subtopics.title: Iran-Israel Rivalry and the Axis of Resistance
subtopics.summary: Iran and Israel were allies during the Shah's reign, but relations turned hostile after the 1979 revolution, when the new Islamic government broke all ties with Israel. The Revolutionary Guard Corps then built a network of armed groups called the Axis of Resistance to confront Israel and its rivals. Its members include Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and Ansar Allah (Houthis) in Yemen.
facts: Iran and Israel were allies during the reign of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
The Shah was ousted in 1979 and an Islamic State was established in Iran.
The Khomeini government broke all relations with Israel after 1979.
The Shah ordered Khomeini to leave Iran in 1964; Khomeini then led the revolution from Iraq.
Khomeini called America the 'Big Devil' and Israel the 'Little Devil'.
The IRGC created the Axis of Resistance, a network of armed groups.
Hezbollah (Lebanon) was formed to fight Israeli forces that had invaded Lebanon in 1982.
Hamas (Gaza City) is linked to the outbreak of the First Intifada against Israel.
Ansar Allah emerged in Yemen as an opposition movement against President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Iran supports the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon as pressure fronts against Israel.

subtopics.title: Strait of Hormuz and Global Energy Shock
subtopics.summary: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is the only maritime outlet for the Gulf's oil and gas exports. The booklet warns that a blockade could push Brent crude prices up and possibly trigger a global energy crisis. Speculative demand from a risk premium can raise prices even before any supply is actually lost.
facts: The strait lies between Iran (north) and the Musandam Peninsula of Oman (south).
It connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and further to the Arabian Sea.
It is the only maritime outlet for the Persian Gulf's oil and gas exports.
It carries nearly 20% of global oil supply.
About 1/5 of global LNG trade and 1/3 of global fertiliser exports transit this corridor.
Traders add a risk premium, which can create artificial price rises through speculative demand.
Conflict could spill into the Red Sea or Suez Canal, raising transit times and freight costs.
India imports about 85% of its crude oil.
Each $1 rise in oil price adds about $1.5 billion a year to India's import bill.
Nearly 40% of India's crude oil imports and over 80% of its LPG imports pass through the strait.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Talks and Military Strikes
subtopics.summary: Nuclear talks in Geneva collapsed over US demands that Iran dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt uranium enrichment. The joint offensive then used heavy bombers, including US B-2 bunker-buster strikes on Fordow. Iran responded with missiles, including the Sejjil, in strikes on Israeli and US military bases.
facts: The 2015 JCPOA was signed between Iran and the P5+1 group of countries.
Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment to 3.67%.
The US withdrew from the JCPOA unilaterally in 2018 and reinstated sanctions.
Geneva talks collapsed over US demands to dismantle Fordow and Natanz and halt enrichment.
US B-2 bombers used bunker-buster bombs to strike the fortified Fordow facility.
US airstrikes targeted Kharg Island, which handles nearly 90% of Iran's crude oil exports.
Iranian missiles struck near the heavily protected Dimona nuclear research centre.
The US B-1B Lancer, nicknamed 'Bone', was deployed in Operation Epic Fury.
The Sejjil is a two-stage, solid-fuel, medium-range ballistic missile.
The Sejjil is called the 'Dancing Missile' for its high-altitude manoeuvrability.

subtopics.title: Iran's Supreme Leader
subtopics.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei was named Iran's third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei was assassinated, the first hereditary-style transfer since the revolution. The office holds ultimate authority over Iran's political, military and religious institutions. The leader is chosen by the 88-member Assembly of Experts, and the office's authority derives from the doctrine of Velayat-e Faqih.
facts: Mojtaba Khamenei was named the third Supreme Leader after Ali Khamenei's assassination.
This was the first hereditary-style leadership transfer in Iran since the revolution.
The Supreme Leader is Iran's de jure head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
The office oversees national security and foreign policy and influences the election vetting process.
The Supreme Leader's authority derives from Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist).
Ruhollah Khomeini institutionalised this doctrine and was Iran's first Supreme Leader.
The Assembly of Experts is an 88-member clerical body elected by the public.
The Assembly of Experts elects the leader, supervises his performance and can remove him if unfit.
The 1989 constitutional amendment relaxed the earlier requirement that the leader be a Marja.

subtopics.title: India's Energy Security and Reserves
subtopics.summary: India imports about 85% of its crude oil, and a large share of its crude and LPG imports transit the Strait of Hormuz. Its Strategic Petroleum Reserves are meant to cushion supply shocks, with current storage of about 3.37 MMT against a total capacity of 5.33 MMT. The government invoked the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 to ensure LPG availability during the crisis.
facts: India imports about 85% of its crude oil.
Nearly 40% of India's crude oil imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
More than 80% of India's LPG imports also transit the same route.
Qatar supplies nearly half of India's LNG imports.
Global crude oil prices have risen by about $20 per barrel (about 30%).
India's Strategic Petroleum Reserve has a total capacity of 5.33 million tonnes, with about 3.37 MMT in storage.
The Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited manages the SPR under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The global norm is to maintain 90 days of net oil import reserves.
The Essential Commodities Act, 1955 was invoked to ensure LPG availability.
West Asia accounts for 60-70% of India's basmati rice exports.

topics.title: Pakistan Declares Open War on Afghanistan's Taliban Government

subtopics.title: Regime changes in Afghanistan (1973-2021)
subtopics.summary: Afghanistan's political history since 1973 has seen a series of regimes, each shaped by outside powers. The monarchy ended in 1973 and was followed by Soviet-backed communist rule, and Soviet military intervention in 1979 drew Pakistan into supporting Afghan Mujahideen factions. Civil war after 1992 led to Taliban rule, which ended with the US intervention of 2001, and the Taliban regained full control after the US withdrawal in August 2021.
facts: Afghanistan's monarchy ended in 1973.
The nationalist regime was followed by communist rule backed by the Soviet Union.
In 1979 the Soviet Union intervened militarily in Afghanistan.
Pakistan supported Afghan Mujahideen factions during the Soviet intervention.
President Najibullah's government collapsed in 1992, triggering civil war.
The Taliban emerged in 1994 and captured Kabul in 1996.
Pakistan was one of the few countries to recognise the Taliban regime.
After the 9/11 attacks, the United States invaded Afghanistan and overthrew the Taliban.
The new Islamic Republic struggled with insurgency and corruption.
After the US withdrawal in August 2021, the Taliban regained full control.

subtopics.title: Factors behind the open war
subtopics.summary: Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab-Lil-Haq on Afghan military bases, and Afghanistan retaliated with airstrikes on Pakistani targets. The escalation grew out of long-standing disputes over cross-border militancy, the Durand Line and border fencing. Clashes at disputed checkpoints turned these tensions into direct military confrontation.
facts: Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab-Lil-Haq on Afghan military bases.
Afghanistan retaliated with airstrikes on Nur Khan Airbase (Rawalpindi) and 12th Division HQ (Quetta).
The Afghan Taliban is allegedly sheltering Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
TTP is accused of launching cross-border attacks inside Pakistan.
Pakistan recognises the Durand Line as a permanent international border.
Afghan governments have historically disputed the legitimacy of the Durand Line.
Pakistan's border fencing has been resisted by Afghan forces.
Repeated Torkham crossing closures hurt Afghan trade and deepened mistrust.
Pakistan's 'strategic depth' doctrine has been eroded by the Taliban's outreach to India.

subtopics.title: India-Afghanistan ties and projects
subtopics.summary: India and Afghanistan share historic links, including Gandhara's place among the Mahajanapadas of the Vedic Age and the Bamiyan Buddhas. Afghanistan is also a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia, and India has supported its energy, agriculture, drinking water and democratic institutions through projects. The Zaranj-Delaram Highway helps Afghanistan reach Iran's Chabahar Port while bypassing Pakistan.
facts: Gandhara, part of modern-day Afghanistan, was one of 16 Mahajanapadas in the Vedic Age.
The Bamiyan Buddhas highlight the influence of Buddhism in Afghanistan.
Afghanistan is a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia, and between South Asia and the Middle East.
TAPI (Peace) Pipeline: a 1814 km gas pipeline from the Galkynysh Gas Field in Turkmenistan through Afghanistan, Pakistan and India.
Salma Dam (Afghan-India Friendship Dam), 2016, in Herat Province, supports energy and agriculture.
Zaranj-Delaram Highway (2009) connects Afghanistan to Iran's Chabahar Port and was built by India's Border Roads Organization.
Shahtoot Dam Project (2021) aims to provide drinking water to Kabul.
Afghan Parliament Building (2015), built by India, symbolises India's commitment to Afghan democracy.

subtopics.title: Implications for India
subtopics.summary: The Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict has several implications for India, touching its western border, its security and its trade routes. Escalation may reduce Pakistan's infiltration pressure along the LoC, but prolonged instability could let ISIS-K regroup and jeopardise India's access to the INSTC. India condemned Pakistan's attacks and reaffirmed support for Afghanistan's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.
facts: India condemned Pakistan's attacks and reaffirmed support for Afghanistan's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.
LoC relief: escalation on the western border may compel Pakistan to reduce infiltration pressure along the LoC.
Terror spillover: prolonged instability risks allowing ISIS-K to regroup and expand across South Asia.
Connectivity risks: the conflict jeopardises India's access to the INSTC and Central Asian trade outreach.
Refugee pressure: a full-scale conflict risks an Afghan refugee inflow onto India's borders.

topics.title: Nepal Election: RSP's Victory and Implications for India

subtopics.title: RSP Victory and the Gen Z Shift
subtopics.summary: The Rastriya Swatantra Party, led by Balendra Shah, secured a landslide victory in Nepal's General Elections. The win followed the 2025 Gen Z Protests, which toppled the government of KP Sharma Oli. Anger over corruption, unemployment and the state's response to protesters fuelled the political change.
facts: RSP, led by Balendra Shah, secured a landslide victory in Nepal's General Elections.
Balendra Shah is Mayor of Kathmandu and is also a rapper.
At 35, Shah is set to become Nepal's youngest Prime Minister.
Shah is a leader of Madhesh descent.
The 2025 Gen Z Protests toppled the government of KP Sharma Oli.
Youth discontent was driven by corruption and elite privileges ('Nepo Kids').
Rising unemployment and lack of accountability added to the frustration.
Government banned 26 social media platforms, cutting off Gen Z's primary medium of expression.
Security forces firing on protesters further escalated anger.

subtopics.title: Nepal's Political System and Parties
subtopics.summary: Nepal is a Federal Democratic Republic with a multi-party system under its 2015 Constitution. Its Parliament is bicameral, and the House of Representatives combines FPTP and PR seats. Political instability is a long-standing feature, and no government has completed a full term since the restoration of democracy in 1990.
facts: The Constitution of Nepal was adopted in 2015.
Nepal is a Federal Democratic Republic with a multi-party system.
The President is the ceremonial head of state; the Prime Minister is head of government.
Parliament is bicameral: House of Representatives and National Assembly.
FPTP: candidate with the highest votes wins. PR: seats allocated by party vote share.
The 275-member House of Representatives has 165 FPTP seats and 110 PR seats.
No government has completed a full term since the restoration of democracy in 1990.
Nepali Congress was founded in 1947, CPN-UML in 1991 and CPN-Maoist Centre in 1994.
KP Sharma Oli, CPN-UML leader, has served as Prime Minister for the 4th time since 2015.
Oli succeeded Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda), who had been Prime Minister since 2009.

subtopics.title: Challenges and Gains for India
subtopics.summary: Shah's assertive nationalism could harden Nepal's stance on the Kalapani-Limpiyadhura dispute and the 1950 Treaty. The decline of traditional parties means New Delhi must rebuild its diplomatic networks. A stable single-party majority and technocratic governance could align with India's Neighbourhood First Policy.
facts: The Kalapani-Limpiyadhura dispute could harden Nepal's stance under Shah's assertive nationalism.
RSP proposes revisiting the 1950 India-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship.
Revisiting the treaty could reduce India's traditional diplomatic leverage in Kathmandu.
Nepal's effort to reduce dependence on India may redirect trade and connectivity projects toward others, including China.
Decline of traditional parties requires New Delhi to rebuild diplomatic networks beyond long-standing channels.
A single-party majority government could provide a stable environment for long-term policy.
RSP's technocratic approach may align with India's Neighbourhood First Policy, especially cross-border rail, power grid and infrastructure.
Madhesh lies in the Terai plains of south-eastern Nepal, bordering the Indian state of Bihar.
Madhesh is often called the 'Granary of Nepal' and has demanded greater political representation.

subtopics.title: India-Nepal Relations and Border Disputes
subtopics.summary: Nepal acts as a Himalayan buffer state between India and China, and the 1950 Treaty forms the base of bilateral ties. Trade, pipeline and rail projects deepen cooperation. Boundary disputes over the Kali river source and Kalapani remain unresolved.
facts: Nepal acts as a Himalayan buffer state between India and China.
Nepal shares a border of 1751 km with 5 Indian states: Sikkim, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
The 1950 Treaty was signed by Indian Ambassador Chandreshwar Prasad Narain Singh and Nepal PM Mohun Shumshere Rana.
India is Nepal's largest trade and investment partner; bilateral trade was $8.5 billion in FY 2024-25.
Motihari-Amlekhgunj Petroleum Pipeline is South Asia's first cross-border petroleum pipeline.
Jayanagar-Kurtha Railway Line is a cross-border rail connectivity project.
Treaty of Sugauli (1816) defined the Kali (Mahakali or Sarda) as the western boundary and the Mechi as the eastern boundary.
Nepal claims Limpiyadhura as the Kali's source; India argues the river rises at Pankhagad, placing Kalapani in India.
Kalapani has been guarded by the Indo-Tibetan Border Police since 1962.
Nepal signed a Belt and Road Initiative framework with China in 2024.

topics.title: India-Canada Relations: Reset, CEPA and Strains

subtopics.title: Background of Bilateral Ties
subtopics.summary: India and Canada established diplomatic ties in 1947 and cooperate in trade, nuclear energy and space. Bilateral trade was worth USD 30.9 billion in 2024. Their nuclear and space links date back to the 1950s and 2013.
facts: Diplomatic ties established in 1947.
Bilateral trade worth USD 30.9 billion in 2024.
Nuclear Cooperation Agreement (2013) facilitates uranium supply and oversight.
Canada assisted India in building a nuclear research reactor named CIRUS in 1954.
Space collaboration between ISRO and the Canadian Space Agency.
Joint research collaboration exists between the two countries.

subtopics.title: Key Outcomes of the Canadian PM's Visit
subtopics.summary: Canadian PM Mark Carney signalled a reset with India, and formal CEPA trade talks restarted. The visit produced outcomes in energy, climate, technology, agriculture, student mobility and critical minerals. Several outcomes came with a stated target or time frame.
facts: Negotiations on CEPA formally restarted.
Bilateral trade target set at $50 billion by 2030.
Canada's Cameco to supply uranium ore concentrates from 2027 to 2035.
Canada announced intent to join the International Solar Alliance.
Canada to upgrade to full membership in the Global Biofuels Alliance.
ACITI (Australia-Canada-India Technology and Innovation) Partnership launched.
ACITI focus: emerging technologies, digital innovation, advanced manufacturing.
Pulse Protein Centre of Excellence set up at National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management.
Fully funded research internships for 300 Indian students annually.
MoU signed for secure and resilient critical minerals supply chains, aligned with the G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan.

subtopics.title: Diplomatic Strains and Trade Impact
subtopics.summary: Ties deteriorated after PM Justin Trudeau alleged a potential link between Indian agents and the 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar. Both countries expelled diplomats and froze consular services. The rifts stalled CEPA talks, slowed trade and delayed visa processing.
facts: PM Justin Trudeau alleged a potential link between Indian agents and Nijjar's killing in 2023.
Both countries expelled diplomats and froze consular services.
India sees Canada's tolerance of Khalistani separatist groups as a threat to territorial integrity.
Diplomatic rifts stalled CEPA negotiations and slowed bilateral trade.
Diplomatic rifts created uncertainty about Canadian investments in India.
Delays in Canadian visa processing for Indians due to reduced Canadian diplomatic staff.
The standoff may harm India's G20 reputation.
The standoff may complicate relations with Five Eyes allies and a G7 member.

subtopics.title: Khalistan Movement and Its Context
subtopics.summary: The Khalistan movement is rooted in Sikh identity, the 1947 Partition and demands for Punjab's autonomy. Violent episodes such as the Air India bombing and the 1984 assassination of Indira Gandhi shaped the issue. Diaspora-based separatist support abroad keeps the issue alive in India-Canada ties.
facts: Khalsa tradition established in 1699, marking Sikh identity and autonomy.
Partition of India (1947) left Sikhs as a minority, creating dissatisfaction over lost ancestral lands.
Anandpur Sahib Resolution demanded greater autonomy for Punjab.
Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale became the face of Sikh militancy, advocating Khalistan.
Operation Black Thunder: Indian forces removed militants from the Golden Temple.
Air India bombing: Canada-based Sikh extremists bombed a flight.
In 1984, Indira Gandhi's Sikh bodyguards killed her, triggering anti-Sikh riots.
Khalistani groups found support in Canada, the UK, the US and Australia.

subtopics.title: Vienna Conventions on Diplomatic Immunity
subtopics.summary: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) and the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (1963) set the framework for diplomatic and consular ties. They protect diplomats from arrest and legal processes and make diplomatic missions inviolable. Consular officers can perform their duties without interference.
facts: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (1961) sets the framework for diplomatic relations.
Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (1963) sets the framework for consular relations.
Diplomats are protected from arrest and legal processes (diplomatic immunity).
Missions cannot be entered without permission (inviolability of diplomatic premises).
Consular officers can perform duties without interference.
Diplomatic immunity is the key provision protecting diplomats.

subtopics.title: Article 3 and the procedure to rename a State
subtopics.summary: Article 3 empowers Parliament to reorganise States, including changing the name of a State. The Union Cabinet approved renaming Kerala as Keralam under this Article. A renaming Bill needs the President's prior recommendation and is passed by simple majority, without a constitutional amendment.
facts: Article 3 empowers Parliament to reorganise States.
Parliament can form a new State by separating territory from an existing State or by merging States or parts of States.
Parliament can increase or diminish the area of a State, alter its boundaries or change its name.
A Bill to rename a State can be introduced only with the prior recommendation of the President, which is mandatory.
The President acts on the advice of the Union Government.
The President refers the Bill to the concerned State Legislature.
The State Legislature can express its views within a specified period.
The opinion of the State Legislature is not binding.
The Bill is passed by simple majority in both Houses of Parliament.
No special majority or constitutional amendment is required.

subtopics.title: Articles 1, 2 and 4: Union, admission of States and status of such laws
subtopics.summary: Articles 1 to 4 sit under Part I, which deals with the Union and its Territory. Article 1 describes India as a Union of States, and Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish new States. Article 4 makes clear that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368, so they can pass by simple majority.
facts: Articles 1 to 4 fall under Part I, titled Union and its Territory.
India is called a Union even though its Constitution is federal in structure.
Article 1 describes India, that is Bharat, as a Union of States rather than a Federation of States.
Article 1 deals with two things: the name of the country and the type of polity.
Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on terms it thinks fit.
Admission under Article 2 refers to States already in existence; establishment refers to States not in existence before.
Article 4 declares that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368.
Such laws can therefore be passed by simple majority.
Names of States and Union Territories and their territorial extent are in the First Schedule.
At present, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories.

subtopics.title: Integration of Princely States and the 1950 classification
subtopics.summary: At independence, India had British Provinces and Princely States. The Indian Independence Act (1947) gave Princely States three options, and 549 of 552 joined India. The Constitution of 1950 then classified the States and Territories into four parts.
facts: The Indian Independence Act (1947) created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan.
The Act gave Princely States three options: join India, join Pakistan or remain independent.
Of 552 Princely States within India's boundaries, 549 joined India.
The three that refused were Hyderabad, Junagarh and Kashmir.
Hyderabad was integrated by police action.
Junagarh was integrated by means of a referendum.
Kashmir was integrated by Instrument of Accession.
Part A: 9 erstwhile Governor's Provinces of British India.
Part B: 9 erstwhile Princely States with legislatures; Part C: erstwhile Chief Commissioner's Provinces and some Princely States.
Andaman and Nicobar Islands were kept as a solitary Part D territory.

subtopics.title: Linguistic reorganisation: commissions and the 1956 Act
subtopics.summary: The demand for linguistic States led to several commissions. The Dhar Commission favoured administrative convenience, the JVP Committee rejected language as a basis, and the Fazl Ali Commission broadly accepted language. The States Reorganisation Act (1956) then created 14 States and 6 Union Territories on 1 November 1956.
facts: The Dhar Commission (June 1948), chaired by SK Dhar, examined reorganisation on the linguistic factor.
The Dhar Commission recommended administrative convenience rather than the linguistic factor.
The JVP Committee (Dec 1948) consisted of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The JVP Committee formally rejected language as the basis for reorganisation of States.
The Fazl Ali Commission, a 3-member body, was appointed to re-examine the question in December 1953.
The Fazl Ali Commission broadly accepted language as the basis but rejected One Language - One State.
The Fazl Ali Commission suggested 16 States and 3 Centrally Administered Territories.
The States Reorganisation Act (1956) and a related amendment created 14 States and 6 Union Territories on 1 November 1956.
Andhra State (1953) was created by separating Telugu-speaking areas from Madras State.

topics.title: SC Ruling on Creamy Layer Determination for OBCs

subtopics.title: 2026 SC ruling on creamy layer
subtopics.summary: In March 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining creamy layer status of OBCs. The Court found that children of government employees are assessed by parental rank or post, while children of PSU and private-sector employees are assessed mainly on parental income, and called this unequal. The Court favoured a post-based criterion across all sectors, while critics point to the absence of a uniform private-sector hierarchy and to the role of income in access to opportunities.
facts: Supreme Court ruled parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for creamy layer status of OBCs (March 2026).
Creamy layer principle excludes socially and economically advanced OBC members from reservation benefits.
Children of government employees are evaluated on parental rank or post.
Children of PSU and private-sector employees are assessed primarily on parental income.
The Court called this unequal method inconsistent and a violation of the principle of equality.
Court proposed a post-based criterion (Group A, B, C or D) as the primary factor for PSU and private-sector parents.
Rank or position in employment reflects social status and influence better than income alone.
Critics: private sector lacks a uniform rank hierarchy, making post-based classification difficult.
Critics: high-income private-sector families could retain reservation benefits.

subtopics.title: Early history of caste-based reservation
subtopics.summary: The idea of caste-based reservation was first proposed in 1882, and separate electorates appeared under the 1909 Act. The 1951 First Amendment added Article 15(4) to legalise caste-based reservation, after the Champakam Dorairajan case had held such reservations violated Article 15. The 1953 Kalelkar Commission and the 1963 MR Balaji ruling, which kept reservation at 50%, shaped the early framework.
facts: 1882: caste-based reservation first proposed by William Hunter and Jyotirao Phule.
1909: Government of India Act gave elements of reservation through separate electorates.
1932: MacDonald/Communal Award provided separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
Poona Pact abandoned separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
1935: Government of India Act extended separate electorates to Depressed Classes, Women and Labour.
1951: First Constitutional Amendment added Article 15(4).
Champakam Dorairajan vs State of Madras (1951): caste-based reservations held to violate Article 15.
1953: Kalelkar Commission (first Backward Class Commission) identified backward classes other than SCs and STs at national level.
1963: MR Balaji vs State of Mysore: Government ordered to keep reservation at 50%.

subtopics.title: Mandal Commission and Indra Sawhney case
subtopics.summary: In 1979 the Morarji Desai government appointed the second Backward Classes Commission under Article 340, and its 1980 report identified 3,743 castes and recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for OBCs. That recommendation was implemented in 1990, and in 1991 economic criteria were introduced along with a further 10% for poorer higher castes. The Indra Sawhney judgement of 1992 rejected the 10% but upheld the 27% OBC quota with conditions.
facts: 1979: Morarji Desai government appointed the second Backward Classes Commission under Article 340.
The commission was headed by BP Mandal and submitted its report in 1980.
Identified 3,743 castes as socially and educationally backward.
Recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for OBCs.
1990: 27% OBC reservation implemented by the VP Singh government.
1991: preference to poorer OBC sections and 10% reservation for economically backward higher castes.
Indra Sawhney (1992): the extra 10% for higher castes was rejected; 27% OBC reservation was upheld with conditions.
Conditions: total reservation shall not exceed 50%; reservation in promotions not allowed.
Creamy layer introduced and to be excluded while identifying Backward Classes; carry-forward rule for backlog vacancies valid.
A permanent statutory body should examine complaints of over- and under-inclusion in the OBC list.

subtopics.title: Later judgements and economic reservation
subtopics.summary: Later judgements clarified rules on promotions, the 9th Schedule and creamy layer exclusion for SCs and STs. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment of 2019 introduced 10% reservation for EWS, and the 2022 Janhit Abhiyan judgement upheld it. The 106th Amendment Act of 2023 provides one-third reservation for women in Parliament and State Legislatures, which ceases after 15 years.
facts: 2006 Nagaraj case: State not bound to provide reservation in promotions to SCs and STs.
To make such a provision, a State must collect quantifiable data, prove inadequate representation and show no compromise on efficiency.
2007 IR Coelho case: laws placed in the 9th Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to judicial review.
Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy was placed in the 9th Schedule in 1994 by the 76th Amendment Act.
2018 Jarnail Singh case: creamy layer exclusion extends to SCs and STs.
2018 Jarnail Singh case: reservation in promotions does not require quantifiable data on SC/ST backwardness.
103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) provided 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).
EWS reservation was based on a commission for Economically Backward Classes (constituted 2005, report July 2010).
2022 Janhit Abhiyan vs Union of India: 103rd Amendment upheld.
106th Amendment Act (2023): one-third of seats for women in Parliament and State Legislatures; ceases after 15 years.

subtopics.title: National Commission for Backward Classes
subtopics.summary: The National Commission for Backward Classes was set up in 1993 by an Act of Parliament. The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 2018 gave it constitutional status under Article 338B and widened its functions. It consists of a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other members, appointed by the President.
facts: Set up in 1993 by an Act of Parliament.
102nd Constitutional Amendment Act 2018 gave constitutional status to the NCBC.
Article 338B provided constitutional status to the NCBC and increased the scope of its functions.
NCBC is authorised to investigate complaints and welfare of backward classes.
Article 342A empowers the President to specify socially and educationally backward classes in States and UTs.
Composition: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 other members.
Members are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
Conditions of service and tenure are determined by the President.
NCBC can recommend inclusion and exclusion of castes from the OBC list.
NCBC can recommend the income level that excludes the creamy layer from reservation benefits.

topics.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: Definition and Certification Changes
subtopics.summary: The Bill narrows the definition of transgender person and omits Section 4(2) of the 2019 Act, which had recognised a person's right to self-perceived gender identity. Identity would be verified by a Medical Board led by a Chief Medical Officer or Deputy CMO, and the District Magistrate would issue the certificate on the Board's recommendation. Individuals who undergo gender reassignment surgery must apply for a revised gender certificate.
facts: Bill omits Section 4(2) of the Transgender Persons Act, 2019.
Section 4(2) earlier recognised the right to self-perceived gender identity.
Definition keeps socio-cultural identities: Kinner, Hijra, Aravani, Jogta, Eunuch.
Definition covers specified inter-sex variations.
Definition covers congenital variations in sexual traits (genitalia, chromosomes, hormones).
Definition covers persons forced into transgender identity through mutilation or castration.
Removed categories: Trans-Man, Trans-Woman, Genderqueer.
Medical Board led by CMO or Deputy CMO verifies transgender identity.
District Magistrate issues certificate based on the Board's recommendation.
Gender reassignment surgery requires a revised gender certificate application.

subtopics.title: Penal, Reporting and National Council Provisions
subtopics.summary: The Bill expands penal provisions, with life imprisonment for forced mutilation of minors and up to 14 years for forcing children into begging. Medical institutions must report gender-affirming surgeries to the District Magistrate, and certificate holders can change their name in official documents. The National Council for Transgender Persons will include State and UT representatives, with rotational representation across regions.
facts: Life imprisonment for forced mutilation of minors.
Up to 14 years imprisonment for forcing children into begging.
Medical institutions must report gender-affirming surgeries to the District Magistrate.
Certificate holders can change their name in official documents.
National Council to include State and UT representatives.
Representation on the National Council is rotational across regions.
Council members must be of Director rank or above.
Council members are nominated by the Centre Govt.

subtopics.title: Significance and Criticism
subtopics.summary: Supporters say the narrower definition and medical certification target welfare, reduce the discretionary power of District Magistrates, and support a national healthcare database. Critics argue that removing self-identification contradicts the NALSA judgment, that medical verification may pathologise gender identity, and that surgery reporting may affect privacy. They also warn that broad terms could be used against NGOs and healthcare providers.

Mandatory reporting enables a national database for healthcare planning and welfare schemes.

subtopics.title: Legal and Welfare Background
subtopics.summary: Legal recognition of transgender persons in India developed through Supreme Court judgments and the 2019 Act. The NALSA judgment (2014) granted legal recognition and rights, and the 2019 Act provides legal recognition, protection of rights and welfare. Government initiatives include the SMILE scheme, a National Portal for ID cards and certificates, and Garima Greh shelter homes.

Transgender Persons Act, 2019 grants legal recognition and prohibits discrimination.

Garima Greh: government shelter homes offering safe spaces, food and skill development for transgender persons in distress.

topics.title: New GDP Series with Base Year Revised to 2022-23

subtopics.title: Base Year Revision to 2022-23
subtopics.summary: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation released the New National Accounts Series, with the GDP base year revised from 2011-12 to 2022-23. The 2026 revision is the 8th base year revision since 1948-49 and aligns with System of National Accounts 2008 and the IMF Quarterly National Accounts Manual 2017. A base year is the benchmark for measuring real changes in GDP, CPI and IIP over time. Revisions reflect structural changes in the economy, such as digital services expansion, renewable energy growth and changing consumption patterns.

subtopics.title: Improved Data Sources and Methods
subtopics.summary: The new series integrates high-frequency and administrative datasets, including GST collection, vehicle registration data, PFMS, the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises and the Periodic Labour Force Survey. Double deflation adjusts both output prices and input prices, giving a more accurate measure of real value addition in manufacturing and agriculture. The revision brings the National Pension System and the Old Pension Scheme into government sector accounting. Platform workers, digital economy participants and hired domestic workers are now captured.

Vehicle registration data and PFMS are integrated into the new series

Double deflation adjusts both output prices and input prices

GDP now includes the National Pension System and the Old Pension Scheme

subtopics.summary: GDP is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced. It can be calculated by three methods: expenditure, production and income. On the expenditure side, GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government expenditure plus exports minus imports. Real GDP is inflation-adjusted GDP, while nominal GDP is GDP at current prices.

Three methods to calculate GDP: expenditure, production and income

GDP is not an accurate measure of the overall living standard or well-being of a country
Example: 2021 GDP at current prices Rs 1000; 2022 GDP at current prices Rs 1650; 2022 real GDP at 2021 prices Rs 1100

quizzes.title: Iran-Israel Rivalry: Background
quizzes.passage:
Relations between Iran and Israel have passed through sharply different phases. During the reign of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the two countries were allies, and their ties continued for years. This changed with the 1979 revolution, when the Shah was ousted and an Islamic State was established in Iran. The new government broke all relations with Israel and treated it as an enemy. Ruhollah Khomeini, the religious leader behind the revolution, had earlier been a fierce critic of the Shah and had been forced out of Iran. From exile in Iraq, he continued to lead the revolutionary movement, and he developed a strongly anti-Western and anti-Israeli outlook.

The rivalry was not limited to diplomacy. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps built a wider network of armed groups across West Asia. The network was meant to confront Israel, the United States and other rival powers in the region. Its members included organisations in Lebanon, Gaza and Yemen. Each group had its own origin, leadership and political character, yet together they created pressure fronts against Israel. This proxy strategy became one of the main sources of tension in the region and remains central to understanding the present conflict.

quizzes.title: Hormuz and India's Energy Exposure
quizzes.passage:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway that connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and, beyond it, to the Arabian Sea. It is the only maritime outlet for the oil and gas exports of the Persian Gulf, which makes it one of the most critical energy chokepoints in the world. Because so much energy passes through it, any threat to shipping in the strait is watched closely by markets. Traders often add a risk premium when disruption seems possible, and this speculative demand can push prices up before any actual supply is lost. If the conflict spreads to the Red Sea or the Suez Canal, shipping routes would be affected, transit times would increase and freight costs would rise. Supply bottlenecks could follow.

For a large importer like India, such shocks reach the economy in several ways. Higher crude prices widen the import bill, add pressure on the rupee and feed into inflation in transport, fertilisers and manufacturing. The government may absorb part of the shock through excise duty cuts, which can worsen the fiscal deficit. Fuel subsidies for LPG and urea may also rise. Energy-intensive industries face higher input costs and shrinking margins, while a wider current account deficit adds to the strain on the economy.

quizzes.title: Background of the open war
quizzes.passage: Pakistan and Afghanistan have shared a difficult relationship for decades, shaped by changes of government inside Afghanistan and by the border between the two countries. Afghanistan's monarchy ended in 1973 and was followed by communist rule backed by the Soviet Union. Pakistan supported Afghan Mujahideen factions during the period of Soviet military intervention, and later became one of the few countries to recognise the Taliban regime. After the Taliban regained full control in 2021, Pakistan initially welcomed the development, expecting strategic alignment. Tensions soon resurfaced, however, as cross-border militancy continued. Pakistan alleges that the Afghan Taliban is sheltering the TTP, while Afghan governments have historically disputed the legitimacy of the Durand Line, which Pakistan treats as a permanent international border. Afghanistan argues that the agreement behind the line was signed under colonial pressure, while Pakistan says it inherited the boundary after independence in 1947. Clashes at disputed checkpoints escalated into direct military confrontation, and the fighting drew a sharp response from India, which condemned Pakistan's attacks. Pakistan's traditional doctrine of strategic depth has also been eroded, since the Taliban has reached out to India and reduced Pakistan's leverage over Kabul. The result is a conflict in which border disputes, militancy and trade disruption reinforce one another.

quizzes.title: India and Afghanistan ties
quizzes.passage: India's relationship with Afghanistan rests on historical, cultural and developmental foundations. Gandhara, a region that is part of modern-day Afghanistan, was one of the Mahajanapadas of the Vedic Age, and the Bamiyan Buddhas reflect the influence of Buddhism in the country. Afghanistan is also strategically important, because it acts as a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia as well as between South Asia and the Middle East. Over the years, India has backed projects that support Afghanistan's energy, agriculture and drinking water needs, as well as its democratic institutions. Dams, roads and public buildings are among the projects India has built or helped build. One gas pipeline would carry natural gas from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India, while another highway gives Afghanistan a route to a port in Iran that bypasses Pakistan. India has also engaged the Taliban regime at a senior diplomatic level, and these ties have continued even as Afghanistan's political leadership has changed. Afghanistan's position on the border differs, since it does not officially recognise the Durand Line. Repeated closures of the Torkham crossing have also hurt Afghan trade and pushed Kabul toward Iranian routes, which shows how trade and border policy are linked. Taken together, India's engagement covers history, development and trade.

The Rastriya Swatantra Party, led by Balendra Shah, who serves as Mayor of Kathmandu and is also a rapper, has reshaped the country's political map. The shift followed a period of deep anger among young citizens, who felt frustrated by corruption among political leaders, rising unemployment and a lack of accountability. Protests intensified, and the government led by KP Sharma Oli was forced out of power. Authorities responded by restricting online platforms, which left young people with fewer ways to voice their views. Security forces also used harsh measures against demonstrators, and this response further escalated public anger. The state's response to the unrest became a central part of the story. At 35, Balendra Shah is set to become Nepal's youngest Prime Minister. He is a leader of Madhesh descent, and his rise comes after a long history of political instability. Since the restoration of democracy in 1990, no government has completed a full term. The new leadership's approach to foreign policy will matter for neighbouring countries, especially India, which has long been a major partner of Nepal. quizzes.title: Border and Trade Recall
quizzes.passage: India and Nepal share one of the most open and historically rooted relationships in the region. Nepal lies in the Himalayas as a buffer between India and China, and its border touches several Indian states, including Sikkim, West Bengal and Bihar. The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship forms the foundation of bilateral relations, although Nepal now considers it outdated and unequal. Trade between the two countries is large, and India is Nepal's largest trade and investment partner. Connectivity projects include a cross-border petroleum pipeline and a cross-border rail line, which are meant to strengthen economic links. Cooperation also extends to power trade, with a trilateral arrangement that allows Nepal to supply electricity to a third country through Indian territory. Boundary questions remain unsettled, especially in the western sector. A treaty signed after a war between Nepal and the British East India Company set the boundaries, but different maps issued over time created confusion about the source of a river. Several water-sharing agreements from earlier decades remain stalled, which delays important joint projects on rivers that flow between the two countries. Both countries are members of regional groupings such as SAARC and BIMSTEC. Nepal's hill districts have long supplied recruits to Indian Gorkha regiments.

quizzes.title: Integration and early reorganisation
quizzes.passage: At the time of independence, India had two categories of political units: British Provinces and Princely States. The settlement of 1947 created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, and gave the Princely States three options: joining India, joining Pakistan or remaining independent. Most Princely States within India's geographical boundaries joined India, while a few refused to do so. Those that refused were later integrated with India, but not all of them through the same route. The process shows how political boundaries were reshaped in the years after independence. The Constitution of 1950 classified the States and Territories of the Indian Union into four parts. The first part covered the erstwhile Governor's Provinces of British India, and the second covered erstwhile Princely States that had legislatures. The third part covered erstwhile Chief Commissioner's Provinces along with some Princely States. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands formed a separate fourth category by themselves. The debate on reorganising States on the basis of language began soon after independence. In June 1948 the government appointed a commission under SK Dhar to examine the issue, and its recommendations placed administrative convenience ahead of language. A Congress committee later rejected language as the basis for reorganisation. The creation of a new State in 1953 then intensified the demand for language-based States, and the government appointed a three-member commission to re-examine the whole question.

In March 2026, the Supreme Court of India ruled that parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining the creamy layer status of Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The judgement responds to a concern about consistency in how the creamy layer is determined. The Court pointed to an uneven system in which children of government employees are assessed on the basis of parental rank or post, while children of employees in public sector undertakings and the private sector are assessed mainly on parental income. It described this unequal method as inconsistent and in conflict with the principle of equality.

The Court's reasoning rests on the view that rank or position in employment reflects social status and influence better than income alone. It also observed that long years of service may raise salary levels without necessarily improving social standing, especially for lower-level employees. A post-based criterion applied across all sectors could, in its view, provide a fair and consistent way to identify the creamy layer.

The ruling has drawn criticism. Private-sector employers have no standardised rank hierarchy, which makes post-based classification difficult. Critics also argue that income strongly shapes access to quality education and opportunities, and that high-income families in the private sector could keep reservation benefits, limiting opportunities for economically weaker OBC groups.

It revisits how the term transgender person is defined, how a transgender identity is verified and certified, what medical institutions must do in certain cases, how the National Council for Transgender Persons is constituted, and which penalties apply to certain offences. Understanding the debate therefore requires looking at how the new provisions relate to earlier rulings on identity, dignity and privacy. The wider history of these rights in India involves courts, Parliament and the executive, each shaping the rules that apply to the people concerned. quizzes.title: Revised GDP Series Practice
quizzes.passage: Measuring an economy requires a fixed reference period against which later figures are compared. This reference, known as the base year, is used to calculate price-adjusted output, so that changes in the size of an economy are not confused with changes in prices. As economies evolve, a base year that once reflected the production structure gradually becomes outdated. New industries grow, consumer habits shift, and the relative importance of sectors changes. Statisticians therefore revise the base year at intervals, rebuilding national accounts on a newer structure. Each revision also gives an opportunity to improve methods and draw on fresh information. Administrative records, periodic household surveys and financial data can capture activities that older estimates may have missed, such as small unregistered enterprises and digital services. The methods used to remove price effects from output figures can also be refined, which sharpens the estimate of value added in key sectors. International guidelines for national accounts are updated periodically, and revisions help countries keep their figures comparable with global standards. Because gross domestic product guides budget planning, investment decisions and assessments of fiscal health, a revision can change reported growth rates and ratios even when the real economy has not changed. For this reason, official releases usually explain how the new figures were built and why they differ from earlier estimates, so that analysts can interpret trends correctly.

quizzes.title: Data and Methods Check
quizzes.passage: Official statistics are only as good as the information fed into them. Traditional estimates leaned heavily on surveys of large, registered firms, which left many small and informal producers poorly measured. Modern statistical systems therefore combine several sources. Tax collections on goods and services offer a timely view of business activity, while registrations of motor vehicles reflect demand and mobility. Financial management systems record government spending and receipts, which helps in measuring public sector activity. Labour surveys provide information on employment, including work that does not follow a conventional pattern. Such sources help capture household enterprises and digital activity that are hard to observe directly. Measurement also depends on how prices are handled. When output is converted into real terms, a careful price adjustment gives a more accurate picture of value added across the economy. Statisticians must also decide who is counted within the economy, and newer estimates aim to include workers who earn income in unconventional ways. quizzes.title: International Bodies MCQ Set
quizzes.passage: Several international bodies were in the news in March 2026, and their work shows how countries cooperate across borders. The move was linked to concerns about sovereignty and dissatisfaction with the organisation's response to COVID-19. The WHO remains responsible for global public health governance, and India falls under its South-East Asia Regional Office. India also has a role in gender equality forums. Its Women and Child Development Minister represented the country at a session of the Commission on the Status of Women in New York, and India has been re-elected to the Commission. The Commission is the principal intergovernmental body of the United Nations dedicated to gender equality and women's empowerment. In Europe, India and Croatia discussed trade and investment opportunities during talks with the Special Envoy for the Three Seas Initiative, a regional platform of European Union countries located between three major seas. Together, these developments show how governments use global and regional forums to pursue shared goals.

quizzes.title: Environment and Space Recall
quizzes.passage: Environmental and scientific initiatives featured prominently in March 2026. The assessment surveyed 30,000 km of National Highways across 24 States, using high-resolution satellite imagery from Resourcesat-2 and Resourcesat-2A. The index was prepared with the National Remote Sensing Centre of ISRO. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change also launched Him-CONNECT at the World Sustainable Development Summit, aiming to connect scientific research with real-world implementation in the Himalayan region. In wildlife conservation, nine cheetahs from Botswana arrived at Kuno National Park under Project Cheetah. The project is India's flagship wildlife conservation initiative and operates under the umbrella of Project Tiger. The cheetah was a species that had become officially extinct in India, so the project aims to reintroduce it. In space news, NASA confirmed that asteroid 2024 YR4 will not hit the Moon, after updated observations from the James Webb Space Telescope. The asteroid belongs to the Apollo group of near-Earth asteroids, whose orbits cross Earth's orbit. Taken together, these items show how monitoring, research and conservation work side by side.
